What this guide pulls from Dr. Kemp Built from Dr. Walter Kemp's Nephrotic Syndrome and Nephritic Syndrome Parts 1 and 2 (slides + narration; Robbins Basic Pathology, 10th ed.). It follows his emphasis: the three light microscopy / IF / EM fingerprints of the primary nephrotic diseases, the secondary causes he lists, and the lupus classes. Practice questions sit at the end of each section; the summary table is last. beyond source = standard teaching points I added; corrected = source slip fixed.

1. Nephrotic vs Nephritic: The Framework

FeatureNephrotic syndromeNephritic syndrome
ProteinuriaHeavy: >3.5 g/24 h (some sources >3.0 g)Lesser (<3.5 g/24 h)
AlbuminHypoalbuminemia (<3.5 g/dL)Variable
EdemaProminent and generalized, incl. periorbitalPresent, with oliguria
LipidsHyperlipidemia / hypertriglyceridemia, lipiduria—
Blood pressureNot a featureHypertension
Urine sedimentTypically no bloodHematuria: dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts
Kidney functionNo acute kidney injuryAzotemia / oliguria (variable)

Kemp warns that the two can overlap (some FSGS has hematuria and hypertension, some nephritic cases are less classic). Learn the basics; exam stems give enough information.

Kemp's mental model

  • Nephrotic: the glomerulus leaks, but the body doesn't realize it, "the gates are wide open" and protein pours out.
  • Nephritic: the body realizes it is sick and clamps down (hypertension, less urine), so less protein escapes.
  • RPGN: same picture as nephritic plus a striking acute kidney injury (rising BUN and creatinine, oliguria). He sees it as the far end of the nephritic spectrum. Characteristic histology: crescents.

Chain of events in nephrotic syndrome

  1. Protein loss → albumin falls (the main protein lost).
  2. ↓ oncotic pressure → fluid leaks out → edema, generalized and periorbital (loose eyelid tissue fills easily). Different from heart failure, where edema favors the legs.
  3. The body makes more lipoproteins → hyperlipidemia; lipid spills into the urine (lipiduria).

Useful testing

TestWhy
UrinalysisRBC casts are very characteristic of glomerular bleeding (blood leaks into Bowman's space, goes down the tubule, and molds into a cast). A kidney tumor does not make RBC casts.
Blood counts, coagulation panel, renal function, electrolytesSeparate nephrotic from rapidly progressive disease
Liver panelViral hepatitis
GlucoseDiabetes is one of the main secondary causes
ANA, anti-dsDNA, C3, C4Lupus is another secondary cause; complement is consumed
CXR, echo, abdominal ultrasoundEdema/ascites, cardiac cause
Renal biopsyIf it helps management, disease is severe, resistant to treatment, or steroid resistant

Immune complexes reach the glomerulus three ways (his clarification): (1) antibody + antigen combine away from the kidney and the complex deposits; (2) a circulating antigen plants in the kidney and antibody then binds; (3) antibody binds an antigen already in the kidney. A fixed antigen can also draw antibody without forming complexes, the linear anti-GBM pattern.

2. Primary Causes of Nephrotic Syndrome

Primary causeWhere it dominates
Minimal change diseaseChildren (most common by far)
Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)Adults (tied with membranous)
Membranous nephropathyAdults (tied with FSGS)
(Membranoproliferative GN)Overlap: can be nephrotic or nephritic; more often nephrotic
  • Primary = the disease originates in the kidney. Secondary = caused by something else (diabetes, lupus, drugs, infection, tumor).
  • All can affect any age; the table gives the most common setting (minimal change in adults and FSGS in kids both happen).
  • Rule of thumb from Kemp: when two numbers are close (FSGS ~30% vs membranous ~35% in Robbins), treat them as about equal; they vary by facility and population. Learn the 90/10 splits.

3. Minimal Change Disease

FeatureDetail
DemographicsMost common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children
MechanismPossible T-cell factor (a lymphokine toxic to epithelial cells) that damages podocytes; association with Hodgkin disease and thymomas
ClinicalNephrotic syndrome (edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia) with selective proteinuria (essentially just albumin); responds to steroids
Light microscopyNormal (as the name implies)
IFNegative
EMFusion (effacement) of podocyte foot processes, the only abnormality
Silver stain: "no abnormality."
EM: fusion of podocyte foot processes (yellow arrow). No columns or gaps; the processes form one continuous layer.
Fusion is not specificFoot-process fusion is seen in FSGS and probably many glomerular diseases. In minimal change it is the only finding.

Point to ponder: why do pathologists rarely see minimal change biopsies in children?

AnswerBecause it is steroid responsive. A child with nephrotic syndrome is treated with steroids first; if the proteinuria resolves, it is assumed to be minimal change and no biopsy is done. Only steroid-resistant cases get biopsied, and the common explanation then is FSGS.

Kemp's opening question

5-year-old girl, swollen legs and puffy eyelids for a week; 24-h urine protein 4.9 g; low albumin; no blood in urineMost likely: minimal change disease. All of A–D could cause nephrotic syndrome, but minimal change is by far the most common in kids; FSGS is next. New-onset type I diabetes would not look like this at that age.

4. Focal Segmental Glomerulosclerosis (FSGS)

FeatureDetail
DemographicsOne of the most common causes of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults (with membranous); also seen in kids; more common in Black than White patients
MechanismDamage to podocytes; suPAR (soluble urokinase-type plasminogen activator receptor) elevated in ~2/3 of cases. Kemp calls suPAR one of the less important facts
ClinicalNephrotic syndrome, but can have hematuria (25–75%) and hypertension (30–50%); non-selective proteinuria (more than albumin, e.g., immunoglobulins)
Light microscopyFibrosis of a portion of some glomeruli: seen on H&E and trichrome (positive)
IFNegative
EMNo immune complexes (foot-process fusion also present)
Left: normal glomeruli beside one with sclerosis (focal: some but not all glomeruli). Right: sclerosis of only a portion of the affected glomerulus (segmental).
Why both IF and EM are "negative"IF and EM both look for antibody bound to antigen (immune complexes). FSGS has no complex deposition, so both are negative for deposits. Don't confuse that with the negative IF of minimal change; the difference is the scar on light microscopy.

Forms of FSGS

FormNotes
Primary (idiopathic)No identified cause
HIV or heroinAssociated with the collapsing variant
Other glomerulonephritis (e.g., IgA nephropathy, membranoproliferative, post-infectious)Damage and inflammation leave scars
Maladaptation to nephron loss (overwork)Reduced renal mass, obesity, sickle cell disease
HereditaryPodocin or cytoskeletal protein mutations; APOL1 (chromosome 22). Kemp: "don't memorize any of those genes."
A scarred, "worn out" glomerulus of the kind seen in secondary FSGS (capillary tuft barely visible at 6 o'clock; the rest scarred together). Kemp notes this patient did not carry a diagnosis of FSGS.

Collapsing variant

Collapse of the glomerular loop with an expanded Bowman space. Normally the tuft almost touches the capsule.
  • Worst prognosis.
  • More common in African-Americans and HIV-positive patients; associated with heroin.
  • More likely to have hypertension and hematuria than classic FSGS.

Point to ponder: why not "focal segmental glomerulonephritis"?

AnswerThere is no inflammation. It is a scarring (sclerosis) disease: focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. (-itis implies inflammation; the terms are sometimes used loosely, but technically shouldn't be.)
Beyond source beyond sourceThe HIV-associated collapsing form is often called HIVAN. Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in a child is a classic way FSGS comes to attention.

5. Membranous Nephropathy

FeatureDetail
DemographicsOne of the most common causes of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults (with FSGS)
Mechanism70–85% due to antibodies to the phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) on podocytes. No inflammatory cells (no lymphocytes, no neutrophils; not proliferative), so damage is likely complement-mediated via the membrane attack complex (C5b–C9)
ClinicalNephrotic syndrome with non-selective proteinuria; variable degree of proteinuria and variable progression
Light microscopyThickened capillary loops ("wire loops") on PAS (also somewhat on H&E); spikes on silver stain
IFGranular IgG and C3, capillary loop pattern (not mesangial)
EMSubepithelial immune complexes
Left: "wire loop" thickening of the capillary loops (look for circular profiles with thick walls). Right: spikes on silver stain (yellow arrow).
Granular IF along the capillary loops (Kemp: seen at both edges where loops wrap around, unlike the mesangial pattern of IgAN).
EM: yellow arrows = subepithelial deposits; blue arrows = new basement membrane growing between the deposits (the spikes).
How the spikes formBasement membrane grows up between and around the subepithelial deposits. On silver stain the membrane is black spikes and the pale areas between are the deposits. That growth is also why the membrane looks thick on H&E/PAS.
Subepithelial = no inflammationSubepithelial complexes do not trigger inflammation (membranous: no infiltrate). Subendothelial complexes do (membranoproliferative). Kemp's memory trick.

Naming

  • Sometimes called "membranous glomerulonephritis," which is not correct (no inflammation). "Membranous glomerular nephropathy" is the most specific form. Don't get caught on the terms.

Secondary causes

CategoryExamples
InfectionsHepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis. (This is why nephrotic syndrome prompts a viral serology panel.)
MalignancyMelanoma, colon and lung cancer
AutoimmuneSLE (lupus class V), other autoimmune diseases
Inorganic saltsGold, mercury
DrugsPenicillamine, captopril, NSAIDs

Kemp's question

43-year-old man: leg swelling, puffy eyes, 5.4 g/24 h protein, low albumin, high triglycerides; EM shows immune complex deposition; due to a recently started drugAnswer: captopril (membranous nephropathy). Also ask where the complexes sit: subepithelial. Penicillin, hydrocodone, metformin and aminoglycosides are not the classic culprits (the classic trio is penicillamine, captopril, NSAIDs; don't confuse penicillamine with penicillin).

EMFoot-process fusion; no immune complexesNo immune complexesSubepithelial immune complexes

SteroidsRespondOften resistant (hence biopsy)—

His one-slide review gives H&E, IF and EM for each; steroid and demographic rows are from his lecture text. FSGS steroid resistance is implied by his minimal-change point-to-ponder.

7. Secondary Cause #1: Diabetic Glomerulosclerosis

  • By far the main secondary cause of nephrotic syndrome.
  • Names (he gives all four, and how each is built): diabetic nephropathy (kidney disease from diabetes; not specific, since diabetes also causes hyaline arteriosclerosis); diabetic glomerulosclerosis (more specific); nodular glomerulosclerosis (how it looks); Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesion (eponym).
  • Mechanism: oxidative injury and non-enzymatic glycosylation of plasma proteins injure podocytes and drive matrix production (scarring).
  • Clinical: causes ~40% of end-stage renal disease (hypertension and diabetes are the two main causes); occurs in type I and type II; earliest sign is microalbuminuria.
H&E: pink, acellular, eosinophilic nodules (yellow arrows) in the glomeruli.
Trichrome: the nodule stains blue (fibrosis; black arrow).
Kemp: "one of 20 absolutely classic images"Eosinophilic acellular nodules in the glomerulus, highlighted by trichrome.

Points to ponder

Why is microalbuminuria the first sign?The glomerular lesion develops slowly, so the leak begins small (a little albumin) before progressing to nephrotic-range protein.
How do you tell diabetic glomerulosclerosis from amyloidosis?Diabetic nodules are scar, so trichrome stains them blue. Amyloid looks similar but isn't fibrosis, so trichrome won't stain it blue; use Congo red.

8. Other Secondary Causes of Nephrotic Syndrome

CauseKey point
DiabetesThe most common secondary cause (Section 7)
AmyloidosisNodules mimic Kimmelstiel-Wilson, but are amyloid: Congo red, not trichrome
SLEWide range of glomerular forms; can look like membranous (Section 9)
Secondary membranousHepatitis B/C, syphilis; melanoma, colon and lung cancer; gold, mercury; penicillamine, captopril, NSAIDs
Secondary FSGSHIV, heroin, other GN, nephron loss (obesity, sickle cell)
Clinical habitWhen someone with nephrotic syndrome has a neoplasm or starts a new drug, think secondary membranous. Order hepatitis serologies.

9. Lupus Nephritis: The Six Classes

Pathogenesis: deposition of DNA–anti-DNA antibody complexes. All lupus patients have ANA; the more specific antibodies are anti-dsDNA (and anti-Smith). Kemp notes renal disease accounts for about half of lupus deaths. Lupus can present nephrotic or nephritic.

ClassNameFeatures
IMinimal mesangialImmune complexes, no light microscopy changes
IIMesangial proliferativeImmune deposits plus increased mesangial matrix (centered in the mesangium)
IIIFocal lupus nephritisSegmental or global proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells, neutrophil infiltrate; affects some glomeruli (<50%)
IVDiffuse lupus nephritis>50% of glomeruli; endothelial and mesangial proliferation; can produce crescents (RPGN); hypertension, hematuria, moderate proteinuria, renal insufficiency
VMembranous lupus nephritisLooks like primary membranous nephropathy
VIAdvanced sclerosing>90% of glomeruli completely sclerosed; end stage (can't tell what came before)
Read the nameClasses I–II are "mesangial" (like IgAN). III–IV are "nephritis" (inflammation): focal then diffuse. V is membranous. VI is scarred-out. Class IV is one of the main routes to class VI.
Transcript slip correctedIn the narration Kemp sometimes mixes up the numbers (e.g., "class four is the membranous" / "class five is advanced sclerosing"). His slides are right: V = membranous, VI = advanced sclerosing.

Class IV in the images

Diffuse lupus nephritis (H&E): every glomerulus is involved and inflamed (diffuse + nephritis). Hardly any open capillary spaces remain because so many cells fill the tuft (compare minimal change, where capillary lumens are open).
EM: deposits in all three compartments: subepithelial, subendothelial, mesangial. (Labels on the original slide.)
  • Lupus can deposit complexes in any compartment.
  • Expect mesangial deposits in classes I–II; subendothelial in III–IV (inflammatory); subepithelial in V (membranous). Kemp's reasoning, not an absolute rule.

Nephrotic vs nephritic and clinical pearls

TopicRemember
Nephrotic>3.5 g/24 h, albumin <3.5, generalized/periorbital edema, hyperlipidemia, lipiduria; no AKI; no hematuria/HTN
NephriticLess protein, HTN, hematuria (RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs), oliguria/azotemia
RPGNNephritic plus AKI; crescents
Deposit locationSubepithelial = quiet (membranous). Subendothelial = inflammatory (membranoproliferative, lupus III/IV).
Child with nephrotic syndromeTreat with steroids; biopsy only if resistant
Terms-itis = inflammation; FSGS and membranous nephropathy are not "-itis"
BiopsyHelps management; severe; treatment-resistant; steroid-resistant
